title: OmrA sRNA inhibits translation of phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase to impair TCA-cycle flux.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and unpacked the Europe PMC supplement (1.41 MB outer zip -> gkag804_supplemental_files.zip, 858 KB) and opened the only machine-readable file, Supplementary_Table_S4.xlsx (26 KB, 4 sheets). Counted exactly 202 mutation rows across 23 unique bacterial isolates, with columns SAMPLE, CHROM, POS, REF, ALT, DP (read depth), AF (allele fraction), GENE, UPSTREAM_GENE, DOWNSTREAM_GENE, all documented in a 'Description' sheet. Also counted the 'Mutations per gene' sheet: 167 gene rows summing to 202 occurrences. Grepped the whole open-access full text for repository deposits (GEO, SRA, BioProject, ENA, PRIDE, Zenodo, figshare) and found none.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: That Supplementary Tables S1-S3 are lists of oligonucleotides, bacterial strains and plasmids, and that the rest of the supplement PDF (941 KB) is supplementary figures; no PDF text extractor was available on this machine, so I inferred their content from the methods text that cites them. All growth curves, Western blots and gel-shift measurements exist only as figure images, not as numeric source-data tables.

a1_downloadable.note: Supplement downloads freely from Europe PMC with no login; I opened it. But there is no repository deposit at all: the raw whole-genome sequencing reads behind Table S4 were never submitted to SRA or ENA, so only the processed variant calls exist.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Verified in the file: Table S4 has no outcome, phenotype or fitness column. Every one of the 23 isolates is a confirmed suppressor, so any label ('does this mutation suppress OmrA toxicity?') would have to be constructed by inference, and there are no non-suppressor isolates to label as negatives.

a3_inputs_present.note: Verified in the file: the only features are a chromosomal coordinate, a reference base and an alternate base against E. coli MG1655 genome NC_000913.3. No sequence context, no expression values, no growth measurements; everything a model would use as input would have to be fetched from the reference genome and other databases.

a4_units_stated.note: Verified in the file: the 'Description' sheet defines every column, including DP as read coverage and AF as the fraction of reads carrying the mutation. These are the only quantitative columns and both are unambiguous.

a5_enough_rows.note: Verified by counting: 202 mutation rows from 23 isolates, and the biologically meaningful unit is the isolate, not the mutation. Far under the ~1,500-row (or ~400 for classification) floor; the paper's actual finding rests on 12 hfq mutations and 3 ppc 5' untranslated region mutations.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially fits in memory; this is the only Part A item the dataset passes comfortably.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The paper's claims that suppressor mutations clustered in hfq and in the ppc ribosome-binding site match the file: hfq appears 12 times and the ppc-upstream intergenic region 3 times in the 'Mutations per gene' sheet.

a8_label_provenance.note: There is no label to trace. The nearest thing to an outcome is 'this isolate grew despite high OmrA', which comes from a UV-mutagenesis selection screen, i.e. a selection outcome recorded only for survivors, never measured per mutation.

honest_claim_h3: No honest model claim is available: with 202 mutations from 23 selected survivors and no measured outcome per mutation, any model would be describing one selection screen, not a general rule.

plain_idea.one_liner: Considered: use DNA sequence around a mutation to predict whether it rescues growth from small-RNA overexpression toxicity.
plain_idea.train_on: Would have trained on mutations found in bacteria that survived a mutagenesis-and-selection screen, each described by its position and base change in the Escherichia coli reference genome. Verified count: 202 mutations from 23 surviving isolates.
plain_idea.predict: Would have predicted whether a given mutation lets the bacterium grow when the small RNA OmrA is overexpressed. The true answer would come from colony growth in the authors' screen, which is recorded only for survivors, so there are no verified negatives.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: If it worked it would help bacterial genetics labs guess which genes buffer a regulatory insult before running a screen; as it stands the data is far too small to learn anything, and the project's only product would be the observation that suppressor screens of this size are not modellable.

ml_idea: None viable from this paper. The only machine-readable data is a 202-row suppressor-mutation table with no outcome column and no negatives. The adjacent project the paper gestures at - predicting which messenger RNAs a bacterial small RNA represses - cannot be trained from this paper either, because the paper contributes exactly one newly validated interaction (OmrA with the ppc 5' untranslated region); web search also shows that task is already served by several published tools (TargetRNA3, sRNARFTarget, graph-neural-network models), so this paper is at best one extra positive example for someone else's benchmark.

effort.compute_note: Not estimated for a real task because none exists; the whole supplement is 1.4 MB and the only table is 26 KB, which I opened directly in pandas/openpyxl in under a second.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Open Supplementary_Table_S4.xlsx and count rows and unique isolates - 202 and 23. That killed it in one command.

verdict_reason: Classic single-mechanism molecular biology paper: the discovery is one small RNA repressing one messenger RNA, supported by gels and growth curves that exist only as figure images. The one machine-readable file holds 202 mutations from 23 selected survivors, with no outcome column, no negatives and no deposited sequencing reads, so Part A fails on A2 (label must be constructed), A3 (no real input features), A5 (202 rows, 23 isolates) and A8 (no measured per-mutation outcome). Scoring stopped there per the checklist.
